## Abstract

Successful hematopoietic cell transplant requires immunosuppression to prevent graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), a lethal, T-cell-mediated post-transplant complication. The phase 3 BMT CTN 1703 trial demonstrated superior GVHD-free/relapse-free survival for post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PT-Cy)-based GVHD prophylaxis versus tacrolimus/methotrexate (Tac/MTX), but did not improve overall survival. To compare T-cell biology between GVHD prophylaxis regimens, 324 patients were co-enrolled onto BMT CTN 1801 (NCT03959241). We quantified T-cell immune reconstitution using multi-modal analysis, including T-cell receptor (TCR) sequencing of 2,359 longitudinal samples (180,432,350 T-cells). Compared to Tac/MTX, PT-Cy was associated with an early, substantial reduction in TCR diversity that was sustained for 2 years. PT-Cy led to a T-cell reconstitution bottleneck, including reduced thymic output and virus-associated TCRs. Decreased D+14 TCR diversity predicted prevention of chronic GVHD, but also correlated with increased moderate-to-severe infections. This study reveals how distinct immunosuppression strategies have significant effects on the global immune repertoire, underpinning post-transplant clinical outcomes.

## Introduction

Immunosuppression to prevent graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) is fundamental to the efficacy of allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT).1–5 However, T cell-directed immunomodulation creates a clinical paradox: while control of T-cell expansion and activation is essential to mitigate GVHD, appropriate reconstitution of the circulating T-cell pool is critical for recovery of robust immunity post-transplant.6

Several immunosuppressive strategies exist for GVHD prophylaxis.2,7–12 The combination of tacrolimus and methotrexate (Tac/MTX) was historically the most common approach.13,14 Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PT-Cy)-based prophylaxis, as tested in a previously-reported Phase 3 trial (BMT CTN 1703),15 recently emerged as a new standard for reduced-intensity unrelated-donor HCT, predominantly due to its salutary effects on acute and chronic GVHD (cGVHD).

Results of the BMT CTN 1703 trial demonstrated that PT-Cy significantly improved GVHD-associated outcomes at 1 year post-HCT compared to Tac/MTX.15 One-year overall survival, non-relapse mortality and disease-free survival did not differ significantly between the study arms, however, and grade 2 (moderate) infections defined by BMT CTN grading16 were more frequent with PT-Cy. The two-year overall survival and disease-free survival also did not differ significantly (Holtan SG, Bolaños-Meade J, Al Malki MM, et al. Improved Patient-Reported Outcomes with Post-Transplant Cyclophosphamide: A Quality-of-Life Evaluation of BMT CTN 1703. Journal of Clinical Oncology In Press). To investigate the biologic underpinnings of these results, 324 patients were co-enrolled onto BMT CTN 1801, a landmark biology study. Here, we present findings of this study, which identify T-cell diversity as a key underlying biological determinant of the immunologic effects of PT-Cy, and of transplant outcomes. They introduce a paradigm shift in our understanding of the key role that early T-cell diversity plays in shaping the long-term outcomes of HCT.

## Results

### Patient characteristics

A total of 324 patients enrolled on BMT CTN 170315 were co-enrolled onto this study (165 from the PT-Cy arm and 159 from the Tac/MTX arm). To quantify T-cell diversity post-HCT, we measured the TCR repertoire using high-throughput deep sequencing of TCR beta-chains (timepoints listed in Supplementary Table 1, samples obtained shown in Extended Data Figure 1). This methodology identifies the scope of TCR beta chains expressed by T cells, a key metric for T-cell immune competence17,18 (Figure 1). A subset of patients also underwent analysis with multiparameter flow cytometry (Supplementary Table 2; n=40, 20 per treatment arm) at the same time-points used for TCR-Seq, with 13 of these patients also undergoing linked single-cell RNA- and TCR Sequencing (on Days 28 and 365 post-HCT, Supplementary Table 2).

All patients received reduced-intensity conditioning prior to HCT for hematologic malignancies. Transplant characteristics and outcomes were representative of the 1703 companion trial (Table 1 and Extended Data Table 1). All patients received peripheral blood stem cell transplants, the majority (67%) from HLA-matched unrelated donors. The primary endpoint for the BMT CTN 1703 trial, GRFS, was higher in patients receiving PT-Cy. Overall survival and the cumulative incidence of disease relapse were not significantly different between the study arms. Grade 2 (moderate) infections16 were more frequent in PT-Cy recipients, whereas the cumulative incidences of cGVHD requiring immunosuppression, and severe acute (grade III to IV) GVHD were higher with Tac/MTX, as detailed previously.15

### Association between T cell repertoire diversity and post-transplant outcomes

To compare the composition and diversity of the TCR repertoire – the total population of T-cell clones circulating in an individual defined by their unique set of TCRs – we performed high-throughput TCR sequencing of 2,359 samples and 180,432,350 T cells, with a median of 44,077 profiled TCRs/sample. While T cell diversity within the grafts themselves were not different between groups (Figure 2a), after transplant, PT-Cy-treated patients demonstrated significantly reduced TCR repertoire size and diversity versus Tac/MTX. These differences were evident as early as 7 days post-transplant and persisted for up to 2 years across multiple quantitative diversity measures,19 including inverse Simpson diversity, Shannon entropy, richness, and singleton TCRs (“singletons” compare single T-cell clones downsampled to adjust for the number of TCRs sequenced, which was robust to a full range of downsampling thresholds (Figure 2b and Extended Data Figures 2–3). These results demonstrate that the divergence in TCR diversity in Tac/MTX versus PT-Cy was substantial, sustained, and evident early after transplant (with the greatest differences between arms at Day +14, Supplementary Table 3), which raised the hypothesis that early measures of TCR diversity may predict transplant outcomes.

To test this possibility, we stratified all patients – independent of treatment arm – into TCR diversity categories and tested whether TCR diversity itself could predict several of the key transplant outcomes measured in the 1703 study. These results demonstrated that while later time-points (Day 98 and 180) were not predictive of cGVHD and infections (Supplementary Tables 4–5), early TCR diversity (measured at Day 14 post-HCT, the timepoint of greatest divergence in the Tac/MTX versus PT-Cy arms) was associated with both outcomes: Figure 3a demonstrates that patients with low (below the median) versus high (above the median) diversity (Supplementary Table 6) had a lower cumulative incidence of cGVHD requiring immunosuppression (28.9% for higher diversity patients vs. 18.2% for lower diversity patients, 95% confidence intervals [CIs] 21.5 to 36.7 and 12.2 to 25.1, respectively; P=0.035). Early TCR diversity was also associated with the cumulative incidence of grade 2 to 3 (moderate to severe/life-threatening) infections, with higher TCR diversity protective against infection (27.5% for higher diversity patients vs. 45.0% for lower diversity patients, 95% CIs 20.3 to 35.1 and 36.6 to 53.1, respectively; P=0.004)(Figure 3b and Extended Data Table 2), and higher TCR diversity also leading to improved infection-free survival (Figure 3c). Importantly, the incidence of chronic GVHD and Grade 2–3 infections followed similar diversity patterns within each treatment arm, though this analysis had limited power when separated by arm (Extended Data Figure 4a–b). Lower NRM was observed for patients with higher TCR diversity, but the difference did not reach statistical significance (P=0.05, Extended Data Figure 4c). Day 14 inverse Simpson diversity did not predict overall survival (P=0.34, Figure 3d), consistent with lower TCR diversity being linked to both positive (protection against cGVHD) and negative (infection risk) transplant outcomes. It also did not predict relapse risk, (P=0.16, Extended Data Figure 4d) consistent with similar relapse rates measured in the BMT CTN 1703 trial for patients treated with Tac/MTX versus PT-Cy.15

### T-cell repertoire diversity bottleneck emerges following PT-Cy

We next determined which T-cell subsets were altered after PT-Cy. We found a substantial reduction in the size of the T-cell population, with pan-T cell depletion measured by flow cytometry (mean number of T cells/μL at 14 days post-transplant 239.0 for Tac/MTX vs. 19.5 for PT-Cy, P=0.0054, Figure 4a). PT-Cy resulted in a significant reduction in all T-cell populations (including total T cells, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and their subpopulations, CD4 Tregs and γδ T cells) (Figure 4b–d, Extended Data Figure 5–6). This reduction was specific to T cells and not observed for NK or B cells (Extended Data Figure 5). This reduction was most notable early, before Day +60. While all T-cell populations were depleted early after PT-Cy, this regimen resulted in a particularly prolonged deficit in naive CD4 and CD8 T cells compared to Tac/MTX, which persisted for 2 years post-HCT (Figure 4b–c; P=0.002 for CD4 naïve T cells and P<0.001 for CD8 naive T cells).

We next performed combined single-cell RNA/TCR-sequencing to link the phenotype of individual T cells to specific TCR clonotypes. We sampled T-cell clones at day 28 (n = 13) and day 365 (n = 13) post-transplant. After identifying naïve and memory T-cell subsets transcriptionally (Figure 4e and Extended Data Figure 7a), we evaluated the distribution of TCRs across phenotypic compartments. Expanded TCRs, those clonotypes present in larger numbers in a given sample, were found exclusively in memory T-cell subsets. Naïve cell subsets, by contrast, were mostly singleton TCRs (Figure 4e). We were able to identify clones captured in both single-cell and bulk TCR sequencing analysis, with similar results (Extended Data Figure 7b).

Of note, for both Tac/MTX and PT-Cy patients, a significant proportion of T cells from the donor graft contributed to the T-cell compartment for years after transplant (Figure 4f). However, this proportion was significantly higher in Tac/MTX compared to PT-Cy early post-transplant, consistent with early depletion of graft-associated clones arising from cyclophosphamide treatment.

Taken together, these findings suggest that HCT results in a bottleneck effect20–23 on the T-cell repertoire, particularly in PT-Cy relative to Tac/MTX (Figure 4g). A bottleneck occurs when there is a sharp reduction in the size of a population due to external events (such as post-transplant treatment with cyclophosphamide) that results in a significant reduction in that population’s genetic variation20–22, here manifesting as reduced TCR diversity. This bottleneck affected all T-cell subsets along with graft-associated TCRs, and likely is a critical component of the mechanism underpinning the reduction in alloreactive T cells that mediate GVHD with PT-Cy.

### Release of the TCR repertoire bottleneck

After suppression of the T-cell population by PT-Cy, there was delayed expansion of most of the remaining T-cell populations. This was measured by several complementary approaches. First, T-cell proliferation (Ki67 expression) was measured using flow cytometry, which documented a delayed pattern of T-cell proliferation with PT-Cy versus Tac/MTX (for example, naïve CD4 T-cell proliferation peaked at Day 7 with Tac/MTX versus Day 42 with PT-Cy, difference between arms P=0.01 at Day 7 and P=0.008 at Day 42, Figure 5a). The delayed T-cell expansion after PT-Cy was associated with delayed TCR repertoire turnover, detected by quantifying the sharing of TCR clones between successive timepoints using the Morisita Index, a normalized metric ranging from 0 to 1 (with 1 denoting complete repertoire overlap). This analysis revealed that Tac/MTX-treated patients reached a stable TCR repertoire more quickly than PT-Cy treated patients (Figure 5b), with the Morisita > 0.5 by Day 14 (Tac/MTX) versus Day 63 (PT-Cy).

The timing of the bottleneck release after PT-Cy was measured through a sum frequency analysis of Day 28 (Figure 5c) and Day 63 (Figure 5d) clones. While few Day 28 TCR clones were present long-term after PT-Cy, clones that emerge by Day 63 persist, consistent with a bottleneck release between these two timepoints. Together these data demonstrate that, while the total number of T cells after Day 63 is similar between Tac/MTX and PT-Cy, the T cells in PT-Cy originate from a smaller founder population, and expand later, leading to a long-term deficit in T-cell diversity versus Tac/MTX.

Recent thymic emigrants (RTEs) are critical for the recovery of post-transplant T-cell immunity. We measured the number of T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs)24 in PT-Cy versus Tac/MTX patients at 4 timepoints (pre-transplant, Days +28, +98 and +365) to compare the contributions of RTEs to post-transplant TCR diversity. As expected, pre-transplant TREC numbers were similar between arms, but PT-Cy patients demonstrated significantly fewer TRECs on Days +28 and +98, with recovery by 1-year post-transplant. This is consistent with cyclophosphamide causing early post-HCT thymic injury, thus further contributing to reduced post-transplant TCR diversity (Figure 5e).

### Functional effect of reduced T cell diversity on antiviral immunity

We next asked whether the constrained TCR repertoire after PT-Cy limited the extent of virus-specific T cells. TCR classifiers are increasingly available for viral infections, and were used in this study to identify clones associated with cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), SARS-CoV-2, herpes simplex virus (HSV)-1, HSV-2 and parvovirus. The total number of virus-specific singleton TCRs was significantly lower in PT-Cy-treated patients, starting early post-transplant and persisting at least 2 years (Figure 5f). Similar trends were observed for each virus individually (Extended Data Figure 8).

## Discussion

We present the findings of a multicenter longitudinal analysis of T-cell composition in HCT patients allocated to one of two prevailing GVHD prophylaxis strategies. This analysis included evaluation of the T-cell repertoire at a depth and scale not previously achieved.25–30 We discovered major differences in T-cell dynamics depending on the type of GVHD prophylaxis regimen, including a significant decrease in TCR diversity with PT-Cy, which was present as early as 7 days post-HCT and persisted for >2 years. TCR diversity was associated with long-term rates of both cGVHD and infection, independent of treatment arm, with PT-Cy more likely to associate with low TCR diversity than Tac/MTX, likely explaining its more effective control of cGVHD and improved GRFS, and its association with increased Grade 2 (moderate) infections. PT-Cy patients demonstrated early depletion of all T-cell populations, as well as deficits in thymic output, with subsequent T-cell expansion from a more limited pool of T-cell clones. This smaller number of T-cell clones led to long-term constraints on TCR repertoire diversity. This is consistent with a T-cell bottleneck effect20–22 with PT-Cy.

Prior studies of post-HCT immune reconstitution have relied on mouse models or single-regimen, uncontrolled human observational cohorts.31–38 In particular, the biology of PT-Cy has not previously been studied in humans in a randomized, comparative fashion. This mechanistic study linked to a large clinical trial enabled the analysis of over 2,000 samples, providing a sample set of sufficient magnitude to overcome the variability inherent in human data,39 particularly during immune reconstitution, when multiple events occur simultaneously. Furthermore, while retrospective work has compared the composition of T cell populations across transplant approaches,38 this study analyzes the actual diversity of those T cell subsets, linked to cell phenotype, substantially deepening our understanding of the impact of key GVHD prophylactic regimens on post-transplant T cell immunity.

The results of this study elucidate the immunologic trade-offs associated with different GVHD prophylaxis approaches. PT-Cy led to pan-T cell depletion and a long-lasting decrease in overall T-cell diversity compared to transplant patients treated with Tac/MTX, and to transplant donors. This functionally smaller T-cell pool likely mitigates GVHD by limiting the number of T cells that mediate tissue damage.40–43 At the same time, however, this relative T-cell diversity deficit also leads to fewer T cells that could be available to respond to pathogen-associated antigens. It is notable that other than an increase in grade 2 (moderate) infections, the decreased TCR diversity with PT-Cy did not produce major clinical costs, though also did not result in significantly improved overall survival. The opposing effects of decreased TCR diversity may contribute to the lack of significant improvement in overall survival despite the substantial reduction in GVHD with PT-Cy.

The increase in grade 2 (moderate) infections with PT-Cy compared to Tac/MTX was primarily due to bacterial infections early post-transplant.15 This observation highlights the often-overlooked role that T cells play in protective immunity against bacteria,44,45 especially for tissue-based protection against GI tract bacterial translocation. With respect to viral infections, PT-Cy has previously been associated with cytomegalovirus reactivation and disease,46 but the risk of this viral infection (and other viral infections) during this trial was not different between arms, despite decreases in viral-associated T cells with PT-Cy. CMV may have been lessened by the wide use of the anti-CMV drug letermovir.47 As such, PT-Cy may result in different infectious risks in places where letermovir use is less common. This analysis was not powered to detect differences in TCR diversity stratified by type of infection, and this represents an important area of future investigation.

The observation that the decreased TCR diversity with PT-Cy did not lead to increased relapses is notable, and suggests that for the reduced-intensity unrelated-donor HCT studied in the BMT CTN 1703/1801 trials, differences in TCR diversity alone do not drive recurrent malignancy. One hypothesis for a positive impact of PT-Cy on relapse prevention after reduced-intensity HCT relates to the increased exposure to cyclophosphamide in these patients, which could have anti-leukemic effects. Reduced exposure to adjunct immunosuppression in PT-Cy patients by controlling GVHD could also better support graft-versus-leukemia effects. Expanding the analysis of the impact of PT-Cy on transplant outcomes for all conditioning intensities and all leukemia molecular subtypes is merited.

This analysis revealed that TCR diversity early (within 14 days) after HCT predicts key transplant outcomes, raising the potential for early identification of at-risk patients, whether treated with Tac/MTX or PT-Cy. Modification of treatment through, for example, reduction in immunosuppression or augmentation in infection prophylaxis, could be considered. Importantly, our observation of decreased TREC output in the first 100 days post-HCT in patients receiving PT-Cy is in agreement with studies in model organisms documenting direct cyclophosphamide-mediated thymic damage48, and suggests that approaches to support thymic recovery may warrant evaluation in PT-Cy-treated patients.

Together, these data provide novel insights into the biologic underpinnings of GVHD and immune reconstitution after HCT and begin to unravel the essential paradox of allogenic HCT: how to balance the hazard of robust donor T-cell number, diversity and function (GVHD) against their potential beneficial effects (engraftment, reductions in infections, and prevention of leukemia relapse). Deconstructing these biologic phenomena will help to guide future innovations in HCT.

## Methods

### Trial design

This study was a companion to the randomized, Phase 3 multicenter BMT CTN 1703 trial.15 Key objectives included comparing the diversity of the T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire after transplant with Tac/MTX versus PT-Cy, and identifying the effects of T-cell diversity on clinical outcomes. Inclusion and exclusion criteria were the same as the paired BMT CTN 1703 trial. Co-enrollment on BMT CTN 1801 was planned for at least 300 patients (70% of the 428-patient enrollment goal for BMT CTN 1703). Informed consent was obtained from all participants. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the National Marrow Donor Program. Submitted on behalf of the Blood and Marrow Transplant Clinical Trials Network (BMT CTN).

### Biologic Samples

Samples were obtained before preparative conditioning (between 7–14 days before transplant), prior to graft infusion (the day prior to or the day of infusion), weekly through the first 84 days after transplant and then on days 98, 180, 270, 365 and 730 after transplant. After transplant infusion, empty stem cell graft bags or syringes were also obtained and shipped to a central reference laboratory for graft cell isolation. Peripheral blood samples were shipped by each site to the central BMT CTN Repository operated by the NMDP where peripheral blood mononuclear cells, whole blood and plasma were isolated and frozen in separate aliquots from each timepoint.

### T-cell receptor variable beta chain sequencing

Immunosequencing of the CDR3 regions of human TCRβ chains was performed using Adaptive Immunosequencing (Adaptive Biotechnologies, Seattle, WA). Extracted genomic DNA was amplified in a bias-controlled multiplex PCR, followed by high-throughput sequencing. Sequences were collapsed and filtered to identify and quantitate the absolute abundance of each unique TCRβ CDR3 region for further analysis as previously described.17,18,49

### Multiparameter flow cytometry

Samples for flow cytometry were selected from patients without chronic GVHD or relapse, to help ensure their reflection of the immunosuppressive strategies used, rather than immune-mediated transplant outcomes. The overall similarity of immune reconstitution in the flow cytometry cohort compared to all BMT CTN 1801 patients was assessed through longitudinal analysis of total lymphocyte counts, which were similar between groups (Extended Data Figure 5a–b). PBMCs cryopreserved at −150C were thawed slowly into prewarmed (37C) media (RPMI + 10% FBS): 1mL of frozen cells was added dropwise to 1mL of media and serially diluted 1:2 with media until a final volume of 32mL. Cells were strained through a 100um cell strainer to remove clumps, centrifuged at 350g for 10min at 23C, and resuspended in 1mL of media for counting. Viable cells were counted with a Cellometer Auto 2000 Cell Viability Counter (Nexcelom). All cells were stained with LIVE/DEAD Fixable Aqua Dead Cell Stain Kit (ThermoFisher), after which cells were divided in half between two antibody panels: 16-color panel for characterizing T cells and a 14-color panel for characterizing B and NK cells. Flow cytometry data were acquired within 48 hours of staining using a LSRFortessa flow cytometer (BD Biosciences) and analyzed using FlowJo (v10.0.0). T cell subsets were defined as follows: TCM (CCR7+ CD45RA−), TEM (CCR7− CD45RA−), TEMRA (CCR7−CD45RA+), TN (CCR7+ CD45RA+ CD95−), TSCM (CCR7+ CD45RA+ CD95+), Treg (CD4+ CD25+ CD127lo), γδ-T cells (CD3+ γδTCR+). NK cells were defined as CD3− NKp46+. B cells were defined as CD3− CD19+. Antibodies used were the following: CD3−BUV395 (BD Biosciences), CD4-BV786 (BD Biosciences), CD5-BV786 (BD Biosciences), CD8-APC-Cy7 (BD Biosciences), CD14-BUV661 (Invitrogen), CD16-APC (BD Biosciences), CD19-PE (Abcam), CD20-BUV661 (BD Biosciences), CD21-BUV737 (BD Biosciences), CD24-APC-Cy7 (BioLegend), CD25-BB515 (BD Biosciences), CD27-BV421 (BD Biosciences), CD28-BUV737 (BD Biosciences), CD38-BV605 (BD Biosciences), CD45RA−PE-Cy7 (BioLegend), CD56-BB515 (BD Biosciences), CD69-BUV496 (BD Biosciences), CD95−AF700 (BioLegend), CD127-PE (BD Biosciences), PD-1-BV711 (BD Biosciences), CD335-PE-Cy7 (BioLegend), CCR7−BV421 (BD Biosciences), gdTCR-BB700 (BD Biosciences), GranzymeB-APC (BioLegend), HLA-DR-BUV496 (BD Biosciences), IgD-BV711 (BD Biosciences), Ki67-PerCP-Cy5.5 (BD Biosciences). Representative gating is shown in Supplementary Figure 1.

### Single-cell RNA sequencing

A subset of the PBMCs from patients analyzed by flow cytometry who had PBMCs frozen from the leftover graft bag/syringe also underwent scRNA- and TCR-Seq. These PBMCs were enriched for CD3+ T cells through MACS using the Miltenyi human Pan T cell Isolation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec). Approximately 16,500 cells per sample were loaded onto a 10X Chromium Instrument (10x Genomics) according to manufacturer’s instructions. GEX libraries were generated using Chromium Next GEM Chip K Single Cell Kit v2 (10X Genomics) and normalized to 12nM; VDJ libraries were generated using Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 5’ Kit v2 (10X Genomics) and normalized to 3nM. Pooled GEX and VDJ libraries were sequenced on Illumina NovaSeq S4 at the Broad Institute.

Analysis of the 5’ scRNA + TCR data was performed as follows: FASTQ files were aligned with Cell Ranger v7.1.0 using GRCh38 as the reference genome, then imported into Python v3.10.12. Droplets were filtered for protein-coding, TR_C_, and IG_C_ genes per annotations from Ensembl v112. We then performed QC to analyze only cells with a mitochondrial gene expression of less than 10%, between 700 and 6,000 unique genes, and between 1,000 and 25,000 transcripts. We further filtered the genes to those expressed in at least 10 cells and then selected the 7,500 most variable genes (running Scanpy v1.10.2) plus PTPRC and CD3E. To filter for T cells, we performed initial clustering with Scanpy and removed clusters with low CD3E expression. We then performed clustering using an encoding generated with scvi-tools v1.1.5 and removed another 2 clusters low in CD3E expression. For all downstream analyses, we focused on D28 and D365 samples. We manually annotated separate D28 and D365 CD4 and CD8 clusters using a list of T cell marker genes and studying the list of differentially expressed genes within each cluster after batch correcting by patient. For TCR analysis, we extracted clonotype groupings generated by Cell Ranger, which were subsequently aligned with Adaptive TRB CDR3 sequences when appropriate.

### T-cell Receptor Excision Circle (TREC) analysis

Genomic DNA extracted for TCR sequencing was subjected to TREC analysis. TREC concentrations were analyzed by real-time quantitative PCR (Bio-Rad) using TaqMan Gene Expression Master Mix (Applied Biosystems). The RT-qPCR reactions were performed in a final volume of 25 μL following the protocol described by Sempowski et al.50. Where possible, 10 μL of sample were loaded into each well. In each reaction, the DNA sample was tested in duplicate. A standard curve was included in each qPCR plate. The number of TRECs/well was normalized to the amount of DNA/well.

### Statistical analysis

TCR diversity was expressed as the inverse Simpson diversity index, as specified in the BMT CTN 1801 Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP). Additional diversity metrics were also explored, as described in Supplemental Methods. Log-normalized diversity values were compared between treatment arms using a mixed-effects model to account for repeated measures with missing values, followed by Fisher’s least significant difference tests at each timepoint. The following additional variables were also tested as candidate covariates for stepwise inclusion in a multivariate model, as specified in the SAP, but none reached the inclusion threshold of P <0.05 (Supplementary Table 7): gender, race, age, primary disease, conditioning regimen, disease risk index (DRI), and degree of HLA match. Associations between TCR diversity and clinical outcomes were assessed as described below. Overall survival, relapse and non-relapse mortality were specified in the SAP; cGVHD and grade 2–3 infection were examined due to their identification in BMT CTN 1703 as key discriminators between the Tac/MTX and PT-Cy arms, results that became available after the SAP was developed. Landmark analyses were performed using day 98 and day 180 diversity values, as specified in the SAP. Exploratory analyses stratifying patients by Day 14 diversity were also performed as this timepoint demonstrated the largest differences in TCR diversity between the Tac/MTX and PT-Cy arms (Supplementary Table 3).

### Diversity Metrics

The number of unique TCR clonotypes identified in a sample is defined as the richness of that sample. To incorporate information about the evenness of the distribution of different clonotypes, additional metrics are calculated. The inverse Simpson diversity index represents the probability of two TCRs chosen at random from the sample being different; larger values reflect a more even distribution of more clonotypes. Shannon Entropy also incorporates both species richness and evenness, but is more sensitive to the number of clonotypes present while being less sensitive to clonotype dominance.19 Singletons are TCRs found exactly once in a sample. The ratio of singletons to richness represents the proportion of unique TCR clonotypes that were found exactly once rather than multiple times in a sample.

### Associations between TCR diversity and clinical outcomes

As specified in the Statistical Analysis Plan, landmark analyses were undertaken at day 98 and 180. To test associations between TCR diversity and clinical outcomes, patients were stratified into high and low diversity groups using the median inverse Simpson diversity value at each specified timepoint, including only patients who had a sample available at those timepoints. The cumulative incidence of each outcome developing subsequent to that timepoint was assessed. ## Abstract

Tissue-specific T cell immune responses play a critical role in maintaining organ health but can also drive immune pathology during both autoimmunity and alloimmunity. The mechanisms controlling intratissue T cell programming remain unclear. Here, we leveraged a nonhuman primate model of acute graft-versus-host disease (aGVHD) after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation to probe the biological underpinnings of tissue-specific alloimmune disease using a comprehensive systems immunology approach including multiparameter flow cytometry, population-based transcriptional profiling, and multiplexed single-cell RNA sequencing and TCR sequencing. Transcriptional profiling revealed substantial biological differences between T cells infiltrating the lung and liver during aGVHD. These included enrichment for transcriptional pathways controlling extracellular matrix remodeling and chemotaxis in the lung and enrichment for transcriptional pathways linked to nucleic acid metabolism and proliferation in the liver. Single-cell RNA sequencing and TCR sequencing substantiated divergent organ-specific transcriptional programing of tissue-infiltrating T cells, which was linked to clonal expansion, with expanded clones progressively enriched for C-X3-C motif chemokine receptor 1 (CX3CR1)–expressing CD8 effector T cells in the lung and eomesodermin (EOMES)–expressing CD8 effector-memory T cells in the liver. This divergent evolution of T cells was maintained even for T cells sharing the same TCRs, indicating its independence from antigen specificity. Together, these results provide insights into the role that tissue microenvironment–derived signals play in local T cell transcriptional programming during alloimmune-mediated clonal expansion and suggest potential opportunities to develop tissue-specific therapeutics to curtail pathogenic immunity after transplant.

## INTRODUCTION

During homeostasis, as well as during immunopathology, the tissue-based T cell immune response has two components. First, organs are dynamically surveyed by T cells that circulate through the peripheral blood and lymphatics. Second, local and autonomously maintained tissue-resident T cells coordinate both healthy and pathogenic immunity (1–3). Both of these T cell populations play integral roles in establishing tissue homeostasis and antipathogen and antitumor protection (4, 5) but, when maladaptive, can cause autoimmune and alloimmune disease (6), including graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) after hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HCT) (7–12). Previous studies of GVHD and other diseases have identified that organ-associated T cells display key tissue-specific characteristics, such as expression of chemokine receptors (13, 14), retention molecules (15), and master transcriptional (16–18) and metabolic regulators (19–21). However, the mechanisms by which organ-specific T cell programming occurs remain uncertain. Given that multiple organs are targeted by pathogenic T cells during GVHD, this disease can serve as a valuable model for how tissue specificity evolves during alloimmunity.

Murine models, which often leverage T cell receptor (TCR)–transgenic T cells to identify tissue-resident cells, including in models of alloimmunity (8, 10, 22–24), have established the foundation for understanding mechanisms controlling T cell trafficking and tissue residency. To more closely recapitulate human T cell tissue–based alloreactivity, driven by polyclonal T cell populations, nonhuman primate (NHP) models can add substantial value (25–29), given their evolutionary proximity to humans (30), the fact that they are outbred, and because they share many of the environmental factors that strongly influence tissue immunity, particularly in barrier organs (31). In this study, we leveraged the NHP acute GVHD (aGVHD) model in rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) (7, 32–34) to interrogate organ-specific T cell transcriptomic patterns that accompany this disease. We have previously identified fundamental qualities of T cells that traffic to canonical aGVHD target organs, including the gastrointestinal (GI) tract (7), the liver (35), and the lungs (36, 37). Although the GI tract is one of the principal aGVHD target organs, recent work from our group (7) has underscored the fact that of these three tissues, the GI tract is characterized by major distinctions compared with the lungs and liver, whereas the two latter organs share important characteristics that position them as ideal comparators for determining organ-specific adaptations to the tissue microenvironment. This prior study used serial intravascular antibody staining (SIVS) (7, 38), which enabled leukocyte tracking on the basis of the time-resolved serial administration of anti-CD45 antibodies conjugated to distinct fluorochromes. This strategy generated a detailed map of immune cell migration and tissue compartmentalization and was used to establish key biologic parallels between the lungs and the liver during aGVHD. These parallels included rapid replacement of organ-associated recipient T cells with those of donor origin and a similar distribution of T cells between the three SIVS-defined tissue compartments: vasculature associated, actively infiltrating, and intratissue (38), with most of the T cells present in the liver and the lung being vasculature associated (7). Unlike the liver and the lungs, the GI tract demonstrated substantially longer persistence of recipient cells and resulting mixed donor chimerism after HCT and was also characterized by a predominance of intratissue T cells rather than vasculature-associated or actively infiltrating T cells (7, 39). Because of these differences, comparisons with the GI tract may be prone to confounding. In contrast, the shared immune landscape of the lung and liver has enabled the current studies, focused on organ-specific T cell programing after HCT.

Here, we used multiple system immunology approaches, including multiparameter flow cytometry, bulk transcriptomics, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and single-cell TCR sequencing (scTCR-seq), to define both shared and organ-specific T cell pathogenic programs in the lung and the liver. Using these techniques, we provide robust evidence linking intratissue clonal expansion to organ-specific T cell programing, connecting these two key cellular processes to lung- and liver-specific immunopathology.

## RESULTS

### aGVHD in NHPs presents with lung and liver pathology

To study the mechanisms by which organ-specific T cell specification occurs during aGVHD, we used the NHP transplant model and performed our analysis on days +7 to 8 after transplant in an aGVHD cohort [using both sibling and nonsibling, major histocompatibility complex (MHC) haploidentical transplant pairs] and in an autologous HCT (auto-HCT) control cohort (fig. S1A; demographic characteristics of study animals are shown in data file S1). Given the colony mating strategies used for rhesus macaques, nonsibling animals are highly likely to be related as cousins or other members of the same family tree (40–42). We have previously reported (33) that, in the absence of immunoprophylaxis, the NHP MHC haploidentical HCT model results in severe aGVHD, for which the target organs include the GI tract, skin, liver, and lungs (7, 32–34). We have previously established key biologic similarities between the lungs and the liver during aGVHD, which provided an essential foundation for the current experiments (fig. S1, B to E). The similarities between the lung and liver include rapid replacement of organ-associated recipient T cells with those of donor origin (with 92 ± 3% donor CD4 T cell chimerism and 95 ± 2% donor CD8 T cell chimerism in the lungs and 95 ± 2% donor CD4 T cell chimerism and 97 ± 1% donor CD8 T cell chimerism in the liver in the current study; fig. S1B). Then, using SIVS (fig. S1C) (7, 38), we found a similar distribution of T cells between the three SIVS-defined tissue compartments: vasculature associated, actively infiltrating, and intratissue (fig. S1, D and E) (7). Histopathologic analysis of the liver (Fig. 1, A and B) and lungs (Fig. 1, C to E) documented the intra- or perivascular nature of T cell infiltration into these two organs, with periportal triad inflammation in the liver [median liver pathology score for aGVHD = 2.5 versus auto-HCT controls = 0.25 or untransplanted healthy controls (HCs) = 0.75, P < 0.0001; Fig. 1B] and an increase in circumferential perivascular inflammation in the lungs [median vascular inflammation (VI) index (36, 43) for aGVHD = 20 versus auto-HCT = 0 or HC = 0, P < 0.001; Fig. 1D] as well as associated interstitial pneumonitis (median interstitial pneumonitis index for aGVHD = 10 versus auto-HCT = 0 or HC = 0, P < 0.01; Fig. 1E).

### T cells infiltrating the lungs and liver during aGVHD display similar phenotypes

We focused our flow cytometry–based analysis on between-organ comparisons of T cell phenotypes in recipients with aGVHD, in auto-HCT controls, and in HCs. This strategy highlighted the similarities, rather than the differences, between broad T cell subsets infiltrating the lung and the liver during aGVHD, despite some differences at baseline or after auto-HCT (Fig. 2, A and B, and data file S2). Thus, as defined by flow cytometry–based immunophenotyping, the T cell infiltration into the liver and lungs during aGVHD was primarily driven by CD8 T cells with an effector-memory (TEM) phenotype (CD8+/CD45RA−/CCR7−) (Fig. 2A) and CD4 T cells with a central memory (TCM) phenotype (CD4+/CD45RA−/CCR7+) (Fig. 2B). Most CD8 and CD4 T cells also expressed CD69, an early marker of tissue residency, with some cells also expressing CD103, a canonical resident memory T cell (TRM) phenotypic hallmark (Fig. 2, C and D). Moreover, CD4 and CD8 T cells infiltrating both the lung and liver during aGVHD similarly up-regulated the proliferation marker Ki67 compared with both the auto-HCT and HC cohorts and expressed a high amount of the cytotoxicity marker granzyme B (which has been shown to mark activated alloreactive CD8 T cells in the NHP aGVHD model) (Fig. 2, E and F) (44, 45). In addition to manual flow cytometry gating, we also used unsupervised FlowSOM (flow cytometry data analysis using a self-organizing map)–based clustering of an aggregated blood, liver, and lung T cell census to analyze the flow cytometry data (46). FlowSOM resolved 14 discrete T cell metaclusters (mc) on the basis of expression of CD4, CD8, CD45RA, CD69, CD95, CCR7, OX40, and programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) (Fig. 3, A and B). We found that, in pretransplant HC samples, the distribution of T cells between metaclusters displayed organ-specific patterns: For example, mc-01 (which represents CD8+CD69+PD-1− TEM cells) was more enriched for liver T cells, whereas mc-03 [CD4+CD69+ TEM cells reexpressing CD45RA (TEMRA cells)], mc-06 (CD4+CD69− TEMRA cells), mc-12 (CD4 CD69+ TCM cells), and mc-14 (CD4+CD69−OX40+ TEM cells) were more enriched for lung T cells. However, during aGVHD, there were fewer FlowSOM-defined phenotypic differences between T cells in the lung and liver, with only one cluster (mc-03, CD4+CD69+ TEMRA cells) still significantly [false discovery rate (FDR) q = 0.003] enriched in the lung versus the liver (Fig. 3, C to E, and fig. S1F). These data demonstrate that at the magnitude of broad T cell phenotypes, the lungs and liver were quite similar during aGVHD, although they could be distinguished by the abundance of CD4 TEMRA cells expressing the tissue-residency marker CD69 (mc-03).

### Bulk transcriptomic analysis provides evidence for liver- and lung-specific T cell programming during aGVHD

Both population-based and single-cell transcriptomics revealed major differences in the gene expression profiles of lung-versus liver-infiltrating T cells during aGVHD. The first analysis performed used NHP-specific gene arrays (Fig. 4A) to determine the transcriptional profiles of CD3+ T cells purified from the lungs, livers, and blood from NHPs with aGVHD [n = 7 (lungs), 9 (livers), and 8 (blood)], after auto-HCT (n = 4 each from lungs, livers, and blood), and from HCs [n = 9 (lungs), 10 (livers), and 23 (blood)]. Using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP, Fig. 4B) and hierarchical clustering (Fig. 4C), we assessed the relationship of the normalized gene expression in the three cohorts. This revealed subclustering of T cell transcriptomes in both an organ- and cohort-specific manner. Differential expression (DE) analysis using an absolute fold-change (FC) cutoff of >1.5 further confirmed the existence of both shared and distinct transcriptomic signatures between aGVHD and auto-HCT (data files S3 to S5) and between the lungs, liver, and blood (Fig. 4D).

We identified 779 DE genes that were overlapping between the liver and lungs (Fig. 4D) by comparing the aGVHD and auto-HCT cohorts. Exploration of the published literature on the top 25 up- and top 25 down-regulated genes in this category revealed a predominant association with cell cycle and proliferation (Fig. 4E and data file S6), consistent with the up-regulation of Ki67 protein expression measured by flow cytometry in T cells in both organs (Fig. 2, J and K). We similarly categorized the top 25 up- and top 25 down-regulated genes in the liver- and lung-specific DE lists (Fig. 4, F and G). In the lung, we prominently found genes associated with extracellular matrix remodeling, leukocyte chemotaxis, and the cell cycle (Fig. 4F and data file S7). Of the top 10 genes overexpressed uniquely in lung T cells in the aGVHD group compared with the auto-HCT group, five were chemokines, including C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 10 (CXCL10), CXCL11, CXCL13, C-C motif chemokine ligand 2 (CCL2), and CCL8 (Fig. 4F) (47–49). These molecules have all been shown to participate in aGVHD pathogenesis by recruiting immune cells to target organs but have not been previously identified as discriminatory for lungs (47–53). The top 25 over- and top 25 underexpressed liver-specific DE genes in the aGVHD versus auto-HCT cohorts also included cell cycle genes but, in contrast with the lung, prominently included genes associated with metabolic functions and effector functionalities (Fig. 4G and data file S8). Metascape (54) was also used to explore the tissue-specific pathways exclusively enriched in T cells infiltrating the lung versus liver during aGVHD (Fig. 4, H to J, and data files S9 to S11), which revealed that overlapping liver and lung pathways were almost exclusively associated with cell proliferation (Fig. 4H and data file S9). The lung-specific pathways identified included epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT), extracellular matrix regulation and remodeling, and leukocyte chemotaxis–related pathways (including regulation of growth and negative regulation of locomotion; Fig. 4I and data file S10). Liver-specific pathways included cell proliferation, translation, and cytokine signaling (Fig. 4J), including evidence for the involvement of T helper 17 (TH17)/cytotoxic type 17 T (Tc17)–related cytokines [interleukin −1R1 (IL-1R1), IL-17A, IL-17RE, IL-21R, IL-23R, IL-23A, and IL-26; data file S11] (55). The comparisons between aGVHD versus HC samples closely aligned to those described above for aGVHD versus auto-HCT samples (fig. S2 and data files S12 to S17), resulting in similarly distinct patterns of gene expression. Together, these data identify unique gene expression programs associated with T cell pathogenesis in the lungs versus the liver during aGVHD.

### Single-cell transcriptomic profiling linked to TCR sequencing reveals divergent clonal evolution of T cells in the liver and lungs during aGVHD

scRNA-seq and scTCR-seq enabled us to connect transcriptional programing to TCR clonotype dynamics in the lung and the liver (Fig. 5A). To accomplish this, we first flow sorted CD45+CD3+ T cells from the lungs (n = 5) and livers (n = 5) of aGVHD animals on day +7 after allogeneic HCT (which was the same posttransplant day used for both flow cytometry and microarray analysis), followed by 10X Genomics–based scRNA-seq with deconvolution using the Python scVI package (56). Batch correction was performed for both animal ID and experimental batch using scVI, with data harmonization between cells from different animals successfully achieved (fig. S3). Unsupervised clustering of liver and lung T cells from the aGVHD cohort plotted in UMAP space (Fig. 5, B and C) identified 16 clusters, all containing cells from multiple HCT recipients, demonstrating minimal interindividual variability of our data. However, the two smallest clusters: cluster 14 (0.24% of total T cells) and cluster 15 (0.04% of total T cells) were dominated by T cells from a single animal (fig. S3C). Because of low cell numbers in these clusters, they were not further analyzed. As expected for organ-derived cells, many of the clusters demonstrated enrichment for previously annotated TRM signatures, including those identified by Snyder et al. (57), Kumar et al. (58), and Milner et al. (fig. S4 and data file S18) (59). Whereas 14 of the 16 clusters contained similar proportions of T cells from both the lung and the liver, one scRNA-seq cluster (cluster 1) was significantly enriched for T cells found within the lung (FDR q < 0.0001), and one cluster (cluster 4) was enriched for liver-derived T cells (FDR q = 0.0495) (Fig. 5D and data file S19). Cells in the lung-specific cluster 1 were identified as CD8 T effector cells expressing C-X3-C motif chemokine receptor 1 (CX3CR1), and cells in the liver-specific cluster 4 included CD8 cycling T cells (fig. S3D, with the full list of cluster-specific genes found in data file S20). These results were corroborated by pseudo-bulk DE analysis using the PyDESeq2 package (60, 61), which revealed substantial transcriptomic differences between the lung-versus liver-derived T cell census, with 318 DE genes identified (138 genes enriched in lung T cells and 180 genes enriched in liver T cells; Fig. 5E and data file S21). Metascape pathway analysis (Fig. 5, F and G) of these DE genes identified that pathways enriched in the lung were associated with the inflammatory response [including tumor necrosis factor–α (TNF-α) signaling through nuclear factor κB (NF-κB)], hematopoiesis/leukemogenesis pathways, guanosine triphosphatase–mediated signaling pathways, and EMT pathways (Fig. 5F and data file S22). Genes overrepresented in liver T cells demonstrated enrichment in pathways associated with the cell cycle, nucleic acid metabolism, translation, and E2F- and MYC-driven pathways (Fig. 5G and data file S23).

Having established the presence of organ-specific transcriptional programing during aGVHD, we were able to probe potential mechanisms by which T cells acquired this organ-specific programing. To leverage TCR clone tracking, we paired scRNA-seq with scTCR-seq (62) to determine the extent to which organ-specific gene expression was linked to individual TCR clonotype dynamics. To accomplish this, we first identified 16,392 individual clonotypes from five liver and five lung samples collected from animals with aGVHD. We further distinguished clones by their degree of clonal expansion, labeling them as “unexpanded” (clone size <2 cells per clone) or as “expanded” (clone size >2 cells per clone). The expanded clones were then subdivided by their extent of expansion, into thirds, termed “low expansion,” “mid expansion,” and “high expansion,” respectively. The first strategy we used to analyze liver-specific versus lung-specific gene expression on the basis of clonal expansion was agnostic to individual clonotype identification but, rather, compared the gene expression profiles from the lung and the liver of unexpanded versus increasingly expanded clones on the basis of their cluster compositions (Fig. 6, A and B). We found that organ-specific transcriptional programming became more prominent in highly expanded clones. Thus, for the lung, as clone size increased, we measured a progressive enrichment for CD8 T effector cells expressing CX3CR1 (cluster 1; Fig. 6A), and for the liver, larger clone sizes were increasingly enriched for CD8 TEM cells expressing eomesodermin (EOMES) (cluster 5; Fig. 6B). CD8 T cycling cell clusters, including cluster 4, were enriched in mid- versus low-expanded clones, suggesting that proliferation of T cells may have preceded their differentiation toward EOMES-expressing T cells (enriched in the most clonally expanded population).

### T cell expansion at the magnitude of individual SCs is linked with distinct organ-specific T cell states during aGVHD

Although the experiments described above are suggestive of organ microenvironmental cues influencing T cell pathogenesis that is linked to T cell proliferation, they do have a key limitation. This is that without detailed transcriptomic analysis of clones that are found in both the lung and the liver, there remains an open question about whether the distinct transcriptomic fates of organ-specific T cells are due to their individual antigen specificity rather than local environmental cues. To address this, we probed TCR clones that were found in both organs to determine whether organ-specific gene expression patterns existed even for these shared clones.

For this analysis, we first used scTCR-seq to identify TCR clones that were found in both the lung and the liver. We refer to these as “shared clonotypes” (SCs); we were able to identify 130 SCs (1865 total cells) between the livers and lungs from four aGVHD animals. These SCs were distinguished from clonotypes identified exclusively in either the lung or the liver (but not both), referred to as “unique clonotypes” (UCs, with 11,871 UCs identified). To interrogate the tissue-specific transcriptional states of lung- and liver-infiltrating SC T cells, we used both hierarchical clustering with Euclidean distance testing and Jaccard similarity testing of cluster distribution. For hierarchical cluster analysis, we focused on SCs for which we could identify at least five cells with shared TCRs in each organ (n = 12 clonotypes, 918 total cells) and performed hierarchical clustering within each clonotype, analyzing all cells in both the liver and the lung (Fig. 6C). To quantify the “within” versus “between” organ transcriptomic similarity within clones, we measured the Euclidean distances between directly connected leaves on the hierarchical clustered dendrogram for each SC. We measured higher distances among clones in the liver-to-lung comparisons versus the liver-to-liver and lung-to-lung distances (liver-to-lung distance, mean = 2.30; liver-to-liver distance, mean = 2.01; lung-to-lung distance, mean = 1.98; P = 0.0003; Fig. 6D), consistent with transcriptional divergence even for shared TCR clonotypes between organs. The hierarchical clustering results were corroborated by measuring the degree of cluster-distribution similarity between the lung and liver for each SC using a Jaccard similarity coefficient (63) (JSC; Fig. 6E). The JSC ranges between 0 (completely disparate distribution) and 1 (identical distribution). Of the 130 SCs studied, 48 clonotypes (37%) demonstrated a JSC = 1, indicating completely overlapping clusters and thus high transcriptional similarity, whereas 51 (39%) demonstrated a JSC of between 0 and 1 (indicating only partial overlapping clusters between the liver and lung); we also identified 31 (24%) clonotypes with a JSC of 0, indicating completely nonoverlapping, totally disparate clusters between the liver and lung, consistent with organ-specific transcriptional differentiation even for these SCs (Fig. 6E). Together, these data provide evidence that, at the magnitude of individual clonotypes, divergent T cell transcriptional evolution occurs in the lung and the liver during aGVHD.

Because clonally expanded lung and liver T cells were progressively enriched for clusters 1 and 5, respectively (Fig. 6, A and B), we hypothesized that inferred SC T cell fate trajectories, performed by pseudotime analysis [using the Monocle3 package (64–69)] would also substantiate these divergent cell trajectories. Monocle3 analysis generated three unsupervised partitions of cells (Fig. 6F) for which partition 1 contained the cells of interest [both lung and liver T cells (Fig. 6G)], including CD8 effector T cells expressing CX3CR1 (Fig. 6H) and CD8 TEM cells expressing EOMES (Fig. 6I). Partition 1 was thus selected for downstream pseudotime analysis. Two unsupervised branching points were identified in partition 1 and used as root nodes for pseudotime calculations (Fig. 6J), which were then mapped onto previously annotated scRNA-seq clusters (Fig. 6K). This analysis identified that clusters 1 and 5 populated distinct pseudotime trajectories, consistent with divergent fates of T cells across the lung and liver, even for those with shared TCR clonotypes.

Last, to determine the degree to which clonal expansion was linked with transcriptomic divergence across organs, we calculated a Pearson correlation coefficient for cluster distribution of each clonotype, subdivided by degree of expansion (Fig. 6L and fig. S5A). This analysis demonstrated that, even for SC, the lung versus liver gene expression divergence became more pronounced with increasing degrees of clonal expansion. The Pearson correlation comparing lung with liver was 0.93 for low expansion clonotypes, 0.81 for mid expansion clonotypes, and 0.24 for high expansion clonotypes (Fig. 6L).

We also determined, for both SCs and UCs, the relative cluster enrichment that occurred with clonal expansion. Consistent with our previous analysis of total liver and lung T cells (Fig. 6A), we found similar progressive enrichment of cluster 1 (CD8 effector T cells expressing CX3CR1) for clonally expanding UCs and SCs in the lungs. In the liver, the cluster structure of the SC T cell subsets differed somewhat from the UC structure. Thus, although highly expanded liver SC and UC T cells both demonstrated enrichment for the EOMES+ CD8 effector/memory cluster (cluster 5), there were some differences in the enrichment patterns for the less expanded SC and UC T cells. The mid and low expanded liver UC T cell subsets were more enriched for cluster 0 (GZMA-expressing CD8 TEM) and cluster 4 (PCLAF-expressing cycling T cells), whereas the mid and low expanded SC T cells demonstrated more enrichment for cluster 1 (CX3CR1-expressing effector CD8 T cells), as well as cluster 5 (fig. S5B), suggesting that there may be, at least in part, distinct differentiation signals received for different classes of T cell clones in this organ. Together, this provides quantitative evidence for organ-specific transcriptional evolution linked to clonal expansion for both shared and unique TCR clonotypes during liver and lung aGVHD.

## DISCUSSION

Here, we demonstrated that clonal expansion is linked to organ-specific transcriptomic programing for polyclonal T cells causing aGVHD. Although the role of tissue-resident T cells in aGVHD pathogenesis has been a focus of many studies (8, 39, 70), the mechanisms by which donor tissue–infiltrating T cells attain organ-specific profiles has remained uncertain. Our findings build on recent insights into the profiles of memory T cells in human healthy tissues (2) and the clonal structure of the T cell pool across multiple organs after HCT in patients (71). They combine both population-based and single-cell transcriptomic profiling as well as scTCR-seq to reveal how donor tissue–infiltrating polyclonal T cells evolve in an organ-specific manner during clonal expansion. Our results identify unique T cell gene expression patterns in the lung and the liver and provide evidence that clonal expansion is a central characteristic of T cells that acquire tissue specificity during aGVHD.

These results identified organ-specific transcriptional programming that distinguished the lung and the liver during aGVHD and could have important implications for organ-specific therapeutic targeting. We found that tissue-infiltrating and clonally expanded lung T cells elaborated a transcriptional program including pathways focused on chemotaxis, EMT, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Moreover, multiple chemokines were up-regulated in lung T cells during aGVHD (including CCL2, CCL8, CXCL8, CXCL11, and CXCL13) (47–52), suggesting a mechanism by which recruitment of other immune cells to the lungs could add to the inflammation and alloimmune response during aGVHD. The trigger for the heightened recruitment of immune cells could be linked to conditioning-induced damage of lung tissue, an organ that has been previously demonstrated to be more sensitive to radiation and chemotherapy compared with the liver (37, 72–75). Single-cell clustering identified a CX3CR1-expressing CD8 effector T cell cluster that was overrepresented in lung versus liver T cells, highlighting CX3CR1:CX3CL1 interactions as potentially specific to lung aGVHD pathogenesis. This could occur through receptor:ligand interactions regulating retention of T cells in lung vasculature (76–78), recruitment to the lung parenchyma or airways (79), or improved survival in the inflamed lungs (80). It has been reported that serum CX3CL1 and peripheral blood CX3CR1+ CD8 T cells are both increased in patients with aGVHD (81), consistent with a potential pathogenic role for this pathway. Other lung-enriched pathways identified by both bulk and single-cell–derived pseudobulk transcriptomic analysis included TNF-α–induced NF-κB proinflammatory signaling pathways and EMT. Up-regulation of EMT pathways in lung-infiltrating T cells is particularly interesting, given that EMT is also a key process leading to bronchiolitis obliterans, the pathologic entity that results in end-stage lung disease after both lung transplantation and HCT (82–84). Of note, EMT is typically associated with pulmonary fibrosis, chronic lung allograft dysfunction, and chronic GVHD (cGVHD) (82, 83, 85). Our data provide evidence for a transcriptional program with the potential for EMT that is associated with acute lung GVHD, potentially laying the groundwork for eventual fibrotic remodeling. Our results also identified remodeling of extracellular matrix pathways enriched in T cells during lung aGVHD, which have also been implicated as increasing the risk of developing pulmonary cGVHD after HCT (86, 87).

In contrast, we found that tissue-infiltrating and clonally expanded liver T cells elaborated a distinct transcriptional program, with enrichment for pathways associated with cell proliferation, nucleic acid metabolism, translation, as well as E2F and MYC signaling. These data corroborate previous studies indicating a robust proliferative T cell response in the liver after local encounter with cognate antigens detected in both infectious (88) and alloimmune models (89–91). These gene expression changes affecting cell replication and metabolism could allow for increased proliferation and enhanced survival during the alloreactive response in the liver and perhaps are related to the unique metabolic functions of this organ, wherein liver T cells are exposed to a highly glucose-rich and glycogen-rich environment (92, 93). Of note, liver T cells were also found to up-regulate cytokine signaling–associated pathways, prominently including TH17/Tc17-associated cytokines, providing evidence for these pathways being active in liver aGVHD; these data are contrasted with previous data in mice that suggested that TH17/Tc17-driven pathogenesis may be more prominent in skin and lung aGVHD (94). In addition, the scRNA-seq cluster overrepresented in liver T cells comprised proliferating CD8 T cells expressing the cell cycle–associated proliferating cell nuclear antigen clamp–associated factor (PCLAF) gene (95). These cells were observed to be in the intermediate-expanded cohort of liver-infiltrating T cells, whereas the most highly expanded liver-infiltrating T cells were relatively enriched for TEM cells expressing EOMES, which has been previously associated with clonally expanded liver-resident CD8 T cells (96). Cells within this cluster had low expression of programmed cell death 1 (PDCD1; PD-1), hepatitis A virus cellular receptor 2 (HAVCR2; Tim-3), T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains (TIGIT), IL-10, lymphocyte activating 3 (LAG3), and integrin subunit alpha 2 (ITGA2; CD49b), suggesting that these cells do not represent EOMES-dependent exhausted CD8 T cells or type 1 regulatory T cells (97, 98), respectively, but rather, resemble cytotoxic CD8 T cells with higher expression of granzyme K (GZMK), granzyme M (GZMM), and killer cell lectin like receptor G1 (KLRG1)/B1/D1. Together, these findings suggest that donor CD8 T cells may first proliferate and subsequently differentiate toward a cytotoxic effector phenotype in the liver during aGVHD.

After identifying these organ-specific transcriptomic features, we were able to provide evidence that, in an outbred, polyclonal model of aGVHD, tissue specificity persisted even for shared TCR clonotypes infiltrating both the lungs and the liver. The within-organ versus between-organ divergence increased with clonal expansion, providing compelling evidence for expansion within a given organ being a key feature in the acquisition of organ-specific T cell programming. Our findings provide molecular and cellular evidence for the influence that aGVHD target tissues have on tissue-specific T cell pathogenesis. These data underscore the role that T cell proliferation plays in donor T cell residency in multiple organs. T cells in both the livers and the lungs of animals were enriched for proliferation pathways compared with both HCs and auto-HCT controls, potentially linking this proliferation with organ-specific imprinting. The comparison with auto-HCT controls highlights that proliferation in aGVHD is distinct from that which occurs during homeostatic reconstitution after HCT and is potentially targetable. Whereas many current aGVHD prophylaxis regimens include nontargeted inhibitors of proliferation (methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil), new targeted inhibitors of alloantigen-driven proliferation are now being identified (32, 99, 100), which might be able to more precisely control pathogenic posttransplant proliferation. Our finding that, with more T cell expansion comes greater organ-specific transcriptional programming, can be explained by two mechanisms. In the first, more expansion is linked to more organ “dwell time,” with T cells increasingly exposed to tissue-specific stromal mediators of T cell transcriptional specification. In the second, it is the intratissue proliferation itself that potentiates organ specification, with links between location cues and expansion cues. Although these two mechanisms cannot be distinguished with the current study, identifying the stromal mediators of T cell organ-specific programming would enable this distinction, representing an important avenue for future investigation.

This study has some limitations. First, NHP transplants were performed under conditions of no GVHD prophylaxis (“NoRx”), allowing for fulminant aGVHD development. Considering the measured within-organ effects of proliferation and clonal expansion to developing an organ-specific T cell phenotype, this could be altered or delayed in the clinical setting where prophylaxis regimens will limit T cell expansion. However, our recent work has demonstrated preserved T cell proliferation in the peripheral blood despite calcineurin inhibition and methotrexate (101), suggesting that these intraorgan links may also be preserved. Second, sample size for the shared clonotype analysis was limited: The T cell clonotypes were collected from a portion of the liver or lung after necropsy and are only a representative sample of all T cell clonotypes that were present in the organ during aGVHD, and, thus, sampling bias could have occurred. This sampling bias is also a general limitation of scRNA-seq and scTCR-seq given the limited number of cells interrogated in each experiment. Last, we note that, although comparing the lung and the liver was well justified given our previously reported results (7, 38), including other lymphoid and nonlymphoid GVHD-target organs, particularly the intestine and skin, and the addition of later time points would enable us to more comprehensively deconvolute tissue microenvironment–driven trajectories of alloreactive T cell diversification during pathogenic alloimmune responses.

This study has provided new insights, at the level of individual TCR clonotypes, into the ability of aGVHD target organs to affect T cell programming. These results help explain the disparate pathology often seen between tissues, especially between the lung and other target organs, where the lung is particularly prone to terminal fibrotic changes. They also identify multiple chemokine-chemokine receptor pathways that could specifically target lung-resident T cells, as well as cell cycle and metabolism pathways that could specifically target liver T cell activation. The curation of these organ-specific transcriptional pathways is the necessary first step to guide the development of tissue-targeted prevention and treatment strategies, which may include approaches to limit conditioning-induced target organ damage that could heighten recruitment of immune and inflammatory cells. Last, the discovery that clonal expansion is a common denominator for organ-specific pathogenic evolution, even for shared TCR clonotypes, suggests that T cell alloantigen–driven proliferation pathways may be able to be specifically targeted in a manner that spares T cell–mediated protective immunity, creating a more specific approach for aGVHD control. Moreover, these new mechanistic insights from aGVHD may also be applicable more broadly to include other alloreactive T cell–driven conditions such as solid organ transplant rejection, as well as organ-specific manifestations of autoimmune disease.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Study design

This was a retrospective study in rhesus macaques (M. mulatta) designed to determine the biological role of the tissue microenvironment in reprogramming allogeneic T cell responses during aGVHD in the target organs. Several cohorts of transplant recipients were studied: (i) recipients that underwent an allogeneic HCT where an MHC-haploidentical animal served as donor, which results in the development of aGVHD [n = 12, median age of recipients = 5.5 (range 4 to 8), median age of donors = 6 (range 3 to 11), male:female ratio for recipients = 7:5, for donors = 5:7]; (ii) recipients that underwent an auto-HCT [Auto; n = 4, median age = 4 (range 4 to 12), male:female ratio = 2:2]; and (iii) a cohort of HCs [n = 26, median age = 6 (range 2 to 17), male:female ratio = 18:8]. Demographic characteristics of study animals are shown in data file S1.

Clinical observation and scoring were performed daily on the NHPs undergoing transplant, and upon necropsy, tissues were collected as described below. Flow cytometry and microarray were performed on fresh samples, and scRNA-seq and scTCR-seq were performed on frozen samples on the basis of matched lung and liver tissue availability. All available samples in the aGVHD and auto-HCT cohorts were used in the microarray analysis, and all HC blood samples available for the aGVHD and auto-HCT cohorts before transplant were included, as well as the HC blood and tissues from the HC necropsy cohort. This study was conducted in strict accordance with US Department of Agriculture regulations and the recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health. It was approved by the Biomere Inc., the University of Washington, and the Massachusetts General Hospital Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees. Reagents used in this study are listed in data file S24.

### HCT in NHPs

The methods for NHP HCT have been previously described and are illustrated in fig. S1A (7, 33). Briefly, MHC-haploidentical HCT and auto-HCT recipients underwent pretransplant conditioning with 1040 cGy total body irradiation before transplantation with an apheresis-derived peripheral blood stem cell product. Transplant recipients were not given immunosuppression. Clinical scores for the skin, GI, and liver aGVHD were recorded daily as previously described (33). The animals were euthanized when they met a preset experimental end point on day 8 or prespecified clinical end points. The necropsy and tissue processing procedures have been previously described (7, 34). Briefly, the lungs, livers, and colons were cut into small pieces and digested with deoxyribonuclease I (Millipore Sigma) and type I collagenase (Thermo Fisher Scientific) (for lungs and livers) or with Liberase TL (Roche) and type I collagenase (for colons) at 37°C for 1 hour and passed through a metal strainer and then 100-, 70-, and 40-μm nylon strainers. The resulting cell suspensions were layered into 70 and 30% Percoll gradients, and the leukocytes were collected at the interphase between the layers. The cells were washed and immediately analyzed or cryopre-served in 10% dimethyl sulfoxide in fetal bovine serum and stored in liquid nitrogen.

### Statistical analysis

Individual-level data are presented in data file S25. Datasets were tested for normal distribution using D’Agostino and Pearson test or Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, where appropriate. Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s multiple comparisons posttest, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), or two-way ANOVA with multiple comparisons posttest corrections using a Benjamini-Hochberg FDR were used for comparing multiple groups, where appropriate. Groups were considered significantly different when P or q < 0.05.
